docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
This section documents the major architectural and technological decisions made throughout the project.

The goal is not only to describe the current architecture, but also to capture the reasoning behind important decisions so that future contributors can understand:

  • Why a particular technology was selected.
  • Which alternatives were considered.
  • What trade-offs were accepted.
  • What impact these decisions have on development, operations, scalability, security, and maintenance.

Documenting decisions helps reduce knowledge loss, accelerates onboarding, and provides historical context when revisiting previous choices.

docs.title: Architecture Decision Records (ADR)
docs.text:
Architectural and technological decisions are documented using Architecture Decision Records (ADR).

An ADR is a short document that captures:

  1. The context of a decision.
  2. The available options.
  3. The selected solution.
  4. The rationale behind the decision.
  5. The consequences and trade-offs.

ADRs are immutable historical records. If a decision changes in the future, a new ADR should be created rather than modifying the original one.

Example decisions include:

  • Selection of Django as the backend framework.
  • Selection of PostgreSQL as the primary database.
  • Adoption of Docker for local development and deployment.
  • Authentication and authorization strategies.
  • Hosting and infrastructure choices.
  • Frontend framework selection.
  • API design conventions.

docs.title: Decision-Making Principles
docs.text: When evaluating technologies, the following principles are generally prioritized:

docs.title: Simplicity
docs.text: Prefer solutions that are easy to understand, maintain, and operate.

docs.title: Developer Productivity
docs.text: Favor technologies that enable rapid development while maintaining code quality.

docs.title: Long-Term Maintainability
docs.text: Choose technologies with strong community support, clear documentation, and proven longevity.

docs.title: Operational Reliability
docs.text: Prefer solutions that are well understood and easy to monitor, deploy, and troubleshoot.

docs.title: Scalability
docs.text: Design for expected growth without introducing unnecessary complexity prematurely.

docs.title: Open Standards
docs.text: Whenever practical, favor open-source technologies and widely adopted standards.

docs.title: ADR Structure
docs.text:
Each ADR follows the same structure:

  • Context

  • Problem or requirement being addressed

  • Options Considered

  • Alternative solutions evaluated

  • Decision

  • Chosen solution

  • Consequences

  • Benefits, limitations, and future implications

docs.title: ADR-0001: Use MkDocs Material for Project Documentation
Context
docs.text:
The project requires comprehensive documentation that can be accessed and maintained by a diverse group of stakeholders, including:

  • Software developers
  • Researchers
  • Graduate students
  • Undergraduate students
  • Project managers and coordinators

Not all contributors are technical, and many stakeholders have limited experience with software development practices and source control systems.

The documentation platform must therefore:

  • Be easy to read and navigate.
  • Support collaborative editing.
  • Be version controlled.
  • Evolve alongside the source code.
  • Allow technical documentation, architecture documentation, and operational procedures to coexist in a single location.
  • Be publishable as a public website.

The project also aims to progressively increase contributors' familiarity with modern software engineering practices, including Git and collaborative development workflows.

Additionally, one of the project's partners and subcontractors, FJNR, already maintains and actively uses a mature MkDocs Material documentation framework and associated workflows.

This framework includes:

  • A standardized documentation structure.
  • Established documentation authoring practices.
  • Automated deployment workflows.
  • Staticrypt integration allowing password-protected publication of static documentation.
  • Integrated search capabilities.
  • Responsive design through Material for MkDocs.
  • Automatic translation capabilities through Google Translate integration.

The project team includes contributors with different native languages and varying levels of technical expertise. The ability to automatically translate documentation reduces communication barriers and improves accessibility for all stakeholders.

The project documentation contains technical, operational, and research-related information that should not be publicly accessible without authorization.The documentation platform must therefore support a lightweight access control mechanism while preserving the simplicity and low operational cost of static hosting.

Leveraging an existing and proven documentation framework significantly reduces implementation effort and allows the team to focus on project-specific documentation rather than documentation infrastructure.

docs.title: Option 1: Google Docs
docs.text: Use Google Docs as the primary documentation platform.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Familiar to most researchers and students.
  • Real-time collaborative editing.
  • No technical setup required.
  • Low learning curve.

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• Documentation is disconnected from the codebase.
  • Version history is separated from application changes.
  • Difficult to review documentation changes through pull requests.
  • Limited support for technical documentation structures.
  • Risk of documentation drift over time.
  • Poor integration with software development workflows.

docs.title: Option 2: GitBook
docs.text: Use GitBook as the documentation platform.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Modern user interface.
  • Good documentation authoring experience.
  • Search and navigation capabilities.
  • Low barrier to entry for non-technical contributors.

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• Introduces an external dependency and platform.
  • Documentation remains partially disconnected from the development workflow.
  • Abstracts Git operations away from contributors.
  • Reduces opportunities for contributors to learn Git-based collaboration.
  • Potential synchronization and conflict resolution challenges when documentation and code evolve together.
  • Increased vendor dependency.

docs.title: Option 3: MkDocs with Material Theme
docs.text: Use MkDocs as a static documentation generator with the Material theme.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Documentation is stored directly within the repository.
  • Documentation evolves alongside the source code.
  • Documentation changes can be reviewed through pull requests.
  • Excellent search functionality.
  • Modern and responsive user interface.
  • Simple Markdown-based authoring.
  • Large open-source community and ecosystem.
  • Easy deployment to static hosting platforms.
  • Reuse of an existing documentation framework already maintained by FJNR.
  • Reduced implementation and maintenance effort.
  • Established documentation governance and workflows.
  • Automatic translation support for multilingual teams.
  • Faster onboarding through familiar tooling already used by project contributors.
  • Reduced project risk by relying on a proven solution.
  • Built-in support for documentation protection through Staticrypt integration.
  • Ability to publish documentation as static files while restricting access through a password-protected access wall.
  • No requirement for a dedicated authentication backend or user management system.

Unlike GitBook, MkDocs does not hide Git workflows. Contributors interact directly with the repository, allowing researchers and students to progressively develop Git skills that will improve future collaboration across the project.

By exposing contributors to Git-based workflows early, the project creates opportunities for knowledge transfer and encourages adoption of modern software development practices.

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• Requires basic familiarity with Git.
  • Contributors must learn Markdown.
  • Documentation updates follow the same review process as source code.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The project will use MkDocs with the Material for MkDocs theme as the primary documentation platform.

Documentation will be:

  • Stored in the project's Git repository.
  • Versioned alongside the source code.
  • Published as a static website.

docs.title: Documentation Hosting Strategy
docs.text:
The generated documentation will be hosted using GitHub Pages.

Because the project source code resides in a private monorepository, the documentation deployment process requires a dedicated publication workflow.

A GitHub Action is responsible for:

  1. Building the MkDocs documentation.
  2. Generating the static site artifacts.
  3. Publishing the generated site to a separate public repository.

To support this workflow, a dedicated GitHub App has been created and granted access to both repositories.

This approach allows:

  • The source code repository to remain private.
  • The documentation website to remain publicly accessible.
  • Automated documentation deployment.
  • Separation between source code and published artifacts.

docs.title: Documentation Protection
docs.text:
Although the generated documentation is published through GitHub Pages, access to the content is protected using Staticrypt.

During the deployment process, generated pages are encrypted and wrapped behind a password-protected access wall implemented entirely through static assets and client-side JavaScript.

This approach allows the project to benefit from the simplicity and low operational cost of GitHub Pages while preventing unrestricted access to project documentation.

The Staticrypt integration is inherited from the existing FJNR MkDocs framework and is automatically applied as part of the documentation deployment workflow.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
The selection of MkDocs Material was influenced not only by its technical capabilities but also by the existence of a mature implementation already available within the project's ecosystem.

By adopting a documentation platform already used and maintained by FJNR, the project benefits from:

  • Existing expertise.
  • Established processes.
  • Reusable infrastructure.
  • Proven deployment workflows.
  • Existing multilingual support.
  • Existing documentation protection mechanisms.

This approach accelerates project setup, reduces maintenance costs, and promotes consistency across collaborating organizations.

While Google Docs and GitBook reduce the technical barrier to entry, they also reduce opportunities for contributors to become familiar with Git-based collaboration practices.

MkDocs Material provides an effective balance between:

  • Accessibility
  • Maintainability
  • Technical documentation quality
  • Collaboration
  • Long-term sustainability
  • Contributor skill development

By keeping documentation inside the repository, contributors learn workflows that are directly transferable to software development activities and future project contributions.

The integrated translation capabilities further support collaboration within a multilingual team and improve the accessibility of project knowledge for researchers and students regardless of their preferred language.

docs.title: Positive
docs.text:
• Single source of truth for code and documentation.
  • Documentation evolves together with the application.
  • Improved traceability of changes.
  • Pull request reviews include documentation updates.
  • Contributors progressively gain Git experience.
  • Public documentation can be deployed automatically.
  • Reduced vendor dependency.
  • Strong support for technical and architectural documentation.
  • Reuse of existing FJNR expertise and infrastructure.
  • Reduced project setup effort.
  • Improved accessibility for multilingual contributors.
  • Documentation can be protected without maintaining a dedicated authentication infrastructure.
  • Sensitive project information remains protected while retaining the simplicity of static hosting.

docs.title: Negative
docs.text:
• Contributors must learn basic Git workflows.
  • Documentation contributions require understanding of branch usages.
  • Initial onboarding effort is higher than with Google Docs.
  • CI/CD infrastructure is required for documentation deployment.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
As the project evolves, numerous architectural and technological decisions will be made regarding:

  • Framework selection
  • Database technologies
  • Infrastructure and deployment strategies
  • Security approaches
  • Integration patterns
  • Development workflows
  • Third-party dependencies

Without a structured decision-making process, important context can be lost over time.

Common challenges include:

  • Team members forgetting why a technology was selected.
  • Repeated discussions about previously resolved topics.
  • Difficulty onboarding new contributors.
  • Uncertainty regarding the rationale behind architectural choices.
  • Knowledge loss when contributors leave the project.

The project requires a lightweight and durable method for recording significant decisions and their rationale.

docs.title: Option 1: No Formal Documentation
docs.text: Rely on source code, commit history, and team discussions.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• No additional documentation effort.
  • Minimal process overhead.

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• Decision rationale is often lost.
  • Context is difficult to reconstruct.
  • New contributors have limited visibility into historical decisions.
  • Architectural discussions may be repeated unnecessarily.

docs.title: Option 2: Centralized Design Documents
docs.text: Maintain large architecture documents containing all decisions.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Decisions are documented in a single location.
  • Easier to produce high-level architecture reports.

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• Documents become difficult to maintain.
  • Historical context becomes harder to track.
  • Changes can unintentionally overwrite previous decisions.
  • Large documents often become outdated.

docs.title: Option 3: Architecture Decision Records (ADR)
docs.text: Maintain a collection of small, focused documents, each describing a single architectural decision.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Decisions remain isolated and easy to understand.
  • Historical context is preserved.
  • Decisions can be reviewed independently.
  • New contributors can quickly understand project evolution.
  • Changes are tracked naturally through version control.
  • Industry-recognized practice.

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• Requires discipline to maintain.
  • Creates additional documentation files over time.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The project will adopt Architecture Decision Records (ADR) as the standard mechanism for documenting significant architectural and technological decisions.

Each ADR will describe:

  • The problem or context.
  • The options considered.
  • The selected solution.
  • The rationale behind the decision.
  • The consequences and trade-offs.

ADRs will be stored alongside the project documentation and versioned within the source repository.

docs.title: ADR Format
docs.text:
Each ADR should follow the following structure:

# ADR-XXXX: Title

## Context

...

## Options Considered

...

## Decision

...

## Consequences

...

docs.title: ADR Naming Convention
docs.text:
ADRs shall be numbered sequentially:

ADR-0001-use-mkdocs.md
ADR-0002-adopt-architecture-decision-records.md
ADR-0003-use-django.md
ADR-0004-use-postgresql.md

ADR identifiers are permanent and must never be reused.

docs.title: Positive
docs.text:
• Architectural knowledge remains accessible over time.
  • Decisions become easier to review and audit.
  • Team onboarding is accelerated.
  • Technical discussions can reference documented decisions.
  • Project evolution becomes easier to understand.
  • Historical context is preserved even when decisions change.

docs.title: Negative
docs.text:
• Contributors must invest time documenting decisions.
  • Documentation maintenance becomes an ongoing responsibility.
  • Poorly written ADRs may provide limited value.

docs.title: ADR-0003: Use Django as Backend Framework
Context
docs.text:
The project requires a backend platform capable of supporting:

  • REST APIs
  • Authentication and authorization
  • Administrative interfaces
  • Database migrations
  • Internationalization (i18n)
  • Data management workflows
  • Testing and CI/CD integration
  • Long-term maintainability

The platform is developed within an academic ecosystem involving:

  • Researchers
  • Graduate students
  • Undergraduate students
  • Software developers
  • External collaborators

A key project objective is to facilitate collaboration between professional software developers and academic contributors while ensuring that the resulting platform remains maintainable beyond the initial development phase.

The selected framework should therefore:

  • Be based on technologies familiar to researchers and students.
  • Encourage participation from contributors with varying software engineering experience.
  • Support the integration of research prototypes and proof-of-concepts.
  • Provide strong security and administrative capabilities out of the box.
  • Minimize the amount of custom infrastructure that must be developed and maintained.

docs.title: Option 1: FastAPI
docs.text: FastAPI is a modern Python framework focused on high-performance API development.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Excellent performance.
  • Automatic OpenAPI documentation.
  • Strong typing support.
  • Modern asynchronous programming model.
  • Well suited for API-centric architectures.

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• Smaller ecosystem than Django.
  • Requires additional tooling for administration and user management.
  • Fewer built-in features.
  • More architectural decisions must be made by developers.
  • Less guidance for non-specialist maintainers.

docs.title: Option 2: Flask
docs.text: Flask is a lightweight Python web framework.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Simple and flexible.
  • Easy to learn.
  • Large ecosystem.

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• Many essential components must be assembled manually.
  • Increased maintenance burden.
  • Lack of standardized project structure.
  • Security, administration, and operational tooling must be selected and integrated separately.
  • Higher risk of architectural divergence over time.

docs.title: Option 3: Django
docs.text: Django is a mature Python web framework providing an integrated set of features for web application development.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Mature and battle-tested ecosystem.
  • Excellent ORM and migration system.
  • Built-in authentication and authorization.
  • Powerful administrative interface.
  • First-class internationalization support.
  • Strong security defaults.
  • Extensive documentation.
  • Large talent pool and community support.
  • Predictable project structure.
  • Widely used within the academic and research ecosystem in Montreal.
  • Familiar technology for researchers and students.
  • Facilitates long-term maintainability by non-specialist contributors.
  • More opinionated than lightweight frameworks.

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• Additional functionality may remain unused in API-centric projects.
  • Slightly higher baseline complexity.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The project will use Django as its primary backend framework.

Django will provide:

  • Core application framework.
  • Database access through the Django ORM.
  • Migration management.
  • Authentication and authorization.
  • Administrative tooling.
  • Internationalization support.
  • Security infrastructure.
  • Configuration management.

REST APIs will be implemented using Django and supporting ecosystem libraries where appropriate.

docs.title: Alignment with Academic Expertise
docs.text:
Python is the programming language most commonly used by researchers and students participating in the project.

Most contributors already possess at least a basic understanding of Python through their academic activities, including:

  • Data analysis
  • Scientific computing
  • Machine learning
  • Research prototypes
  • Automation scripts

Selecting a Python-based backend framework lowers the barrier to participation and promotes collaboration between technical and non-technical stakeholders.

It also increases the likelihood that future contributors will already possess relevant knowledge, reducing onboarding costs and improving long-term sustainability.

docs.title: Integration of Research Prototypes
docs.text:
Research projects frequently produce scripts, prototypes, and proof-of-concepts developed by students and researchers.

Python provides exceptional flexibility for integrating these contributions into production systems.

Because Python can be used with varying levels of typing and architectural rigor, professional software developers can progressively adapt research code to production standards without requiring complete rewrites.

This significantly reduces friction between academic experimentation and industrial software development.

docs.title: Adoption within the Academic Ecosystem
docs.text:
Django is widely adopted within universities, research laboratories, and academic institutions in Montreal.

As a result:

  • Existing expertise is readily available.
  • Training resources are abundant.
  • Future collaborators are more likely to be familiar with the framework.
  • Recruiting contributors becomes easier.

Choosing a framework already present within the local ecosystem reduces project risk and promotes knowledge sharing across organizations.

docs.title: Administrative and Security Capabilities
docs.text:
The platform will be maintained over time by a mix of developers, researchers, and students.

Django provides a comprehensive administrative interface out of the box, allowing authorized users to:

  • Manage users.
  • Configure permissions.
  • Inspect project data.
  • Perform operational tasks.
  • Manage reference data and system configuration.

Django also includes many security features by default, including:

  • Authentication mechanisms.
  • Permission management.
  • Protection against common web vulnerabilities.
  • Secure session management.
  • CSRF protection.
  • Password management utilities.

By relying on established framework conventions rather than custom implementations, maintainers benefit from extensive documentation and community guidance.

This reduces the need for contributors to independently design or implement security-critical components and lowers the risk of introducing vulnerabilities.

docs.title: Long-Term Maintainability
docs.text:
The project prioritizes maintainability and knowledge transfer over raw framework performance.

Django's integrated ecosystem reduces the number of third-party components required to operate the platform and provides a clear architectural structure that future contributors can understand and extend.

The framework's maturity and stability reduce long-term technical risk while providing sufficient flexibility for future evolution.

docs.title: Positive
docs.text:
• Strong alignment with the academic ecosystem.
  • Familiar technology for researchers and students.
  • Easier integration of research prototypes and scripts.
  • Mature ORM and migration tooling.
  • Comprehensive administrative interface.
  • Strong security defaults.
  • Extensive documentation and community support.
  • Reduced architectural decision burden.
  • Improved long-term maintainability.
  • Easier onboarding of future contributors.

docs.title: Negative
docs.text:
• Some framework components may remain unused.
  • Additional abstraction compared to lower-level frameworks.
  • Slightly larger application footprint.
  • Less flexibility than assembling a custom stack.

docs.title: Future Considerations
docs.text:
If future requirements demand highly specialized workloads, these concerns should be addressed through:

  • Horizontal scaling.
  • Caching layers.
  • Background workers.
  • Dedicated microservices where justified.

The adoption of Django does not prevent future introduction of specialized services while preserving a consistent and maintainable core platform.

docs.title: ADR-0004: Use PostgreSQL as Primary Database
Context
docs.text:
The project requires a data storage solution capable of supporting:

  • Structured data management
  • Validation and integrity constraints
  • Complex querying
  • Scientific data modelling
  • High collaboration between researchers and developers
  • Long-term maintainability
  • Future analytical and graph-based workloads

A recurring requirement expressed by researchers is the ability to perform graph-oriented analysis and reasoning on project data.

Many of the concepts manipulated by the platform naturally form networks of relationships, including:

  • Activities
  • Processes
  • Resources
  • Organizations
  • Ontologies
  • Dependencies

As a result, graph databases were initially considered a strong candidate.

However, the project must also support numerous features that are not inherently graph-oriented, including:

  • User management
  • Authentication
  • Configuration management
  • Administrative workflows
  • Data validation
  • Reporting
  • Operational tooling

The selected database solution must therefore balance graph capabilities, usability, maintainability, and future flexibility.

docs.title: Option 1: Native Graph Database
docs.text: Use a graph database such as Neo4j as the primary data store.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Natural representation of highly connected data.
  • Powerful graph traversal capabilities.
  • Rich graph query languages.
  • Strong support for graph analytics and inference.

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• Less familiar to researchers and students.
  • Smaller talent pool.
  • Additional learning curve.
  • Less suitable for traditional application data.
  • Increased architectural complexity.
  • More difficult validation and constraint management.
  • Potential need for additional databases for non-graph workloads.

docs.title: Option 2: Relational Database Only
docs.text: Use a traditional relational database as the sole data store.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Mature ecosystem.
  • Strong consistency guarantees.
  • Excellent tooling.
  • Familiar data model.

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• Some graph-oriented queries may be more complex.
  • Less specialized support for graph analytics.

docs.title: Option 3: PostgreSQL as Primary Database with Future Graph Extensions
docs.text: Use PostgreSQL as the primary source of truth while retaining the ability to expose graph-oriented capabilities when required.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Mature relational database platform.
  • Excellent Django integration.
  • Strong validation and integrity mechanisms.
  • Familiar technology for researchers and students.
  • Broad community support.
  • Future compatibility with graph-oriented tooling.
  • Single source of truth for all application data.

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• Native graph capabilities are less specialized than dedicated graph databases.
  • Some advanced graph workloads may require additional tooling.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The project will use PostgreSQL as its primary database and authoritative source of truth.

All application data will be stored and managed within PostgreSQL.

If future graph-oriented requirements justify additional infrastructure, graph capabilities will be introduced as an extension of the PostgreSQL ecosystem rather than by replacing the primary database.

Potential approaches include:

  • PostgreSQL graph extensions such as Apache AGE.
  • Dedicated read-only graph replicas.
  • Analytical graph processing environments.

docs.title: Accessibility for Researchers and Students
docs.text:
While graph databases are increasingly popular in research environments, they remain significantly less familiar than relational databases, particularly for students and occasional contributors.

Most researchers already possess some level of familiarity with:

  • Tables
  • Rows
  • Columns
  • SQL queries

A relational model therefore provides a lower barrier to entry and improves collaboration across multidisciplinary teams.

The resulting data model is easier to understand, explain, document, and validate.

docs.title: Validation and Data Integrity
docs.text:
A core requirement of the platform is ensuring the quality and consistency of data.

PostgreSQL provides extensive support for:

  • Constraints
  • Foreign keys
  • Transactions
  • Uniqueness validation
  • Referential integrity

These capabilities allow the platform to enforce data quality directly at the database level.

Implementing and maintaining equivalent validation logic within graph-centric systems would generally require additional effort and complexity.

docs.title: Existing Graph Capabilities
docs.text:
Although PostgreSQL is primarily a relational database, it already supports several mechanisms that enable graph-oriented operations.

Examples include:

  • Recursive Common Table Expressions (CTEs)
  • Hierarchical queries
  • Relationship traversal through joins
  • Materialized views
  • Advanced indexing

These capabilities provide sufficient graph-like functionality for many use cases without introducing additional infrastructure.

docs.title: Apache AGE Compatibility
docs.text:
A significant factor in the decision is the availability of Apache AGE, an open-source graph extension for PostgreSQL.

Apache AGE allows graph structures and graph queries to be executed directly on top of PostgreSQL.

This means PostgreSQL can evolve toward graph-oriented workloads without requiring a complete migration to a separate database platform.

The project therefore preserves future flexibility while maintaining a simple architecture today.

docs.title: Future Graph Replication Strategy
docs.text:
If future requirements justify a dedicated graph database, PostgreSQL provides an excellent foundation for creating a read-only graph replica.

This approach offers several advantages:

  • PostgreSQL remains the authoritative source of truth.
  • Graph workloads can be isolated from transactional workloads.
  • Researchers gain access to specialized graph tooling.
  • Existing application functionality remains unchanged.

This architecture avoids forcing all project data into a graph-centric model when only a subset of use cases truly benefit from graph traversal.

docs.title: Unified Platform for Mixed Workloads
docs.text:
A significant portion of the platform's functionality is not graph-oriented.

Examples include:

  • User accounts
  • Authentication
  • Permissions
  • Configuration
  • Administrative data
  • Reporting
  • Audit information

Using PostgreSQL as the primary database allows graph-related and non-graph-related features to coexist within a single coherent platform.

This reduces duplication, simplifies operations, and provides a consistent development experience.

docs.title: Positive
docs.text:
• Familiar technology for researchers and students.
  • Lower learning curve.
  • Excellent integration with Django.
  • Strong validation and integrity guarantees.
  • Simplified data modelling and onboarding.
  • Single source of truth for all application data.
  • Future compatibility with graph technologies.
  • Ability to introduce graph databases incrementally.
  • Broad community support and documentation.
  • Improved long-term maintainability.

docs.title: Negative
docs.text:
• Some graph workloads may be less efficient than in specialized graph databases.
  • Additional graph infrastructure may eventually be required for advanced analytics.
  • Future graph replication introduces architectural complexity if adopted.

docs.title: Future Considerations
docs.text:
The project may evaluate the following enhancements as requirements evolve:

  • Apache AGE integration.
  • Read-only graph replicas.
  • Dedicated graph analytics environments.
  • Graph visualization tools.
  • Semantic and ontology-driven reasoning systems.

Any future graph infrastructure should complement PostgreSQL rather than replace it unless a clear operational or scientific benefit is demonstrated.

docs.title: ADR-0005: Use Docker for Development and Deployment
Context
docs.text:
The project requires a consistent and reproducible execution environment across:

  • Local development
  • Automated testing
  • Continuous Integration (CI)
  • Staging environments
  • Production deployments

The application depends on several external components, including:

  • Python runtime
  • Django
  • PostgreSQL
  • System-level dependencies
  • Internationalization tooling
  • Static asset generation

Historically, differences between developer workstations and production environments can lead to issues such as:

  • Dependency mismatches
  • Operating system incompatibilities
  • Undocumented setup requirements
  • Environment-specific bugs
  • Difficult onboarding experiences

The project requires a solution that minimizes environmental inconsistencies while simplifying deployment and maintenance.

docs.title: Option 1: Native Installation
docs.text: Developers install Python, PostgreSQL, and all required dependencies directly on their machines.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• No container runtime required
  • Simpler execution model
  • Lower resource consumption

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• Environment drift between developers
  • Difficult onboarding process
  • Increased support burden
  • Higher risk of "works on my machine" issues
  • Less representative of production

docs.title: Option 2: Virtual Environments Only
docs.text: Use Python virtual environments while installing system dependencies manually.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Standard Python workflow
  • Lightweight setup

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• Does not solve operating system differences
  • System dependencies remain unmanaged
  • Database configuration varies between environments
  • Limited reproducibility

docs.title: Option 3: Docker and Docker Compose
docs.text: Use Docker containers to package application dependencies and Docker Compose to orchestrate local development environments.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Consistent environments across all stages
  • Reproducible builds
  • Simplified onboarding
  • Isolated dependencies
  • Easy integration with CI/CD pipelines
  • Production deployment parity
  • Simplified database provisioning

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• Additional tooling to learn
  • Increased resource usage
  • Longer build times compared to native execution

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The project will use:

  • Docker for application packaging
  • Docker Compose for local development orchestration
  • Multi-stage Docker builds for production images

All development, testing, and deployment workflows should be executable through containerized environments.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
Docker provides a consistent execution environment regardless of the host operating system.

Using containers allows the project to:

  • Define infrastructure as code
  • Eliminate dependency drift
  • Improve reproducibility
  • Simplify onboarding
  • Align development and production environments

Containerization also integrates naturally with modern CI/CD workflows and cloud deployment platforms.

By adopting Docker early, the project avoids future migration efforts and establishes a deployment strategy that scales with project complexity.

docs.title: Development Environment
docs.text:
Local development environments are orchestrated using Docker Compose.

The default development stack includes:

  • Django application container
  • PostgreSQL database container
  • Documentation container (MkDocs Material)

Example services:

  • api
  • db
  • documentation

Developers should be able to start the complete development environment using a single command:

docker compose up

docs.title: Production Environment
docs.text:
Production deployments use the production target defined in the application's multi-stage Dockerfile.

Production images:

  • Exclude build-time dependencies
  • Run as a non-root user
  • Include only required runtime components
  • Execute database migrations during startup
  • Collect static assets automatically
  • Compile localization files when required

The production image should remain deployable independently of the development environment.

docs.title: Continuous Integration
docs.text:
Continuous Integration workflows must validate:

  1. Development image builds successfully.
  2. Django application checks pass.
  3. Database migrations execute successfully.
  4. Automated tests pass.
  5. Production image builds successfully.

This ensures that both development and deployment workflows remain functional.

docs.title: Positive
docs.text:
• Consistent developer experience.
  • Simplified onboarding process.
  • Reduced environment-specific bugs.
  • Improved CI/CD reproducibility.
  • Clear separation between build-time and runtime dependencies.
  • Easier deployment to cloud platforms and container orchestration systems.
  • Infrastructure configuration becomes version controlled.

docs.title: Negative
docs.text:
• Additional Docker knowledge required for contributors.
  • Increased resource consumption on developer machines.
  • Additional maintenance of container configuration files.

docs.title: Future Considerations
docs.text:
Future deployment strategies may include:

  • Kubernetes
  • Docker Swarm
  • Managed container platforms
  • Horizontal scaling
  • Automated image publishing
  • Vulnerability scanning
  • Supply chain security verification

The adoption of Docker does not constrain future infrastructure choices and provides a foundation for more advanced deployment workflows.

docs.title: Règles logiques
docs.text:
• Une activité déclarative peut avoir plusieurs profil d’action
  • Une activité générique est un ensemble de flows générique attaché à la même activité déclarative.
  • Une dimension peut être rattaché à plusieurs profils d’action
  • Un flow générique peut avoir plusieurs profil d’objet
  • Une dimension peut être rattaché à plusieurs profils d’objet
  • Une flow générique doit posséder une provider ou des informations permettant de définir un provider approprié
  • Une flow générique peut posséder un proxy. Si c’est le cas, doit être associé à un proxy existant ou spécifier les informations permettant de définir un proxy approprié

docs.title: Profils
docs.text:
Une tab Profils a été créé pour gérer les différentes éléments qui sont consititués de la meme facon mais font des références à différents niveau de l'architecture Il est obligatoire de spécifier un dimension En suite, il est possible de spécifier une modalité ou une taxonomie par rapport à des règles définit :

  • ExactModality : Juste une modalité
  • SeveralModalities : Plusieurs modalité
  • LeavesOnly :
  • Descendance : La descendance des modalités → besoin de spécifier le niveau de descendance via LevelDescendance
  • AllModalities : Toutes les modalités de la dimension
  • Taxonomy : Un niveau de taxonomies → besoin de spécifier le niveau de taxonomies par rapport à la dimension sélectionnée via TaxonomyLevel

docs.title: ActionProfil
docs.text: Relie un profil à une activité déclarée. Les profils associés ne peuvent être que des profils avec des dimensions de type action

docs.title: Flows
docs.text:
Relie un profil à une flow générique. Un type est également spécifié :

  • Classic : lien direct entre un flow générique et le profil
  • Proxy : le profil associé à ce flow générique est utilisé comme proxy

docs.title: Provider
docs.text:
Dans l'activité générique, un provider doit être spécifier. Pour cela plusieurs facons :

  • Créer un profil de provider ou sélectionner un profil de provider existant → élément d'ActionProfil
  • provider_temporal : Spécifier la temporalité d’un provider
  • provider_location : Spécifier la localisation d’un provider
  • provider_selection_rule : Spécifier le rôle d’un provider dans une liste de choix
  • external_provider_id : Indiquer un id d’un provider issu d’une base de donné extérieur style “ecoinvent”.

Il est obligatoire de spécifier au moins un des deux combinaison pour le provider dans une activité générique

  • provider_id, temporalité, localisation et rôle
  • external_provider_id

docs.title: Proxy
docs.text:
Un proxy sert à remplacer un profil objet par un autre profil objet lorsqu'aucune donnée n'est disponible. Les proxys utilisent les mêmes mécanismes de profils mais sont limités aux dimensions d'objets. La présence d’un proxy est gérée par un boolean. Dans le cas ou il y a un proxy, plusieurs façons de le spécifier dans l’activité :

  • Créer un profil de proxy ou sélectionner un profil proxy existant : tab de jonction GenericActivitesProfils
  • proxy_object_profile_temporal: Spécifier la temporalité d’un proxy
  • proxy_object_profile_location: Spécifier la localisation d’un proxy

Automatiquement, lorsqu'une modalité à plusieurs noms est indiquée, des modalités avec des noms de niveaux plus grands doivent être créées.

docs.title: How this documentation is published
docs.text:
Searching how to publish this documentation ?

Once you push your changes to the main branch, the entire process is automated. Simply commit your updates, and the system will handle the rest seamlessly.

This documentation is publicly accessible, while its source remains private.

This page explains how and why the documentation is published this way, and documents the architectural choices behind it.

docs.title: Context and constraints
docs.text:
We want to:

  • Keep the documentation source private
  • Publish the documentation publicly
  • Avoid any dependency on a personal GitHub account
  • Host everything on GitHub Pages
  • Protect the content behind a password, even though it is publicly hosted

At the same time, GitHub imposes an important constraint:

GitHub Pages on the Free plan can only serve content from public repositories.

This means a private repository cannot directly publish to GitHub Pages.

docs.title: High-level architecture
docs.text:
To satisfy these constraints, we split responsibilities across two repositories:

  • A private monorepo containing:
  • MkDocs source files
  • Build configuration
  • Encryption configuration

  • CI/CD workflow

  • A public hosting repository containing:

  • Only the encrypted static output
  • No documentation source
  • No build configuration

The public repository exists only to serve GitHub Pages.

docs.title: Repositories involved
docs.text:
• Private source repository https://github.com/polariis-plus/polariis-plus-monorepo

  • Public hosting repository (GitHub Pages) https://github.com/polariis-plus/polariis-plus-documentation

  • Published website https://polariis-plus.github.io/polariis-plus-documentation/

docs.title: Documentation build and encryption
docs.text:
The documentation is built using MkDocs and then encrypted using Staticrypt.

Staticrypt performs client-side encryption of the generated static site and injects a password prompt into the final HTML. The result is a set of static files that can safely be hosted on any static hosting provider.

Important characteristics of this approach:

  • The encrypted site can be served as plain static files
  • No server-side logic or authentication is required
  • The password is never stored in the public repository

This provides a lightweight protection layer suitable for internal or semi-private documentation.

docs.title: Publishing from private to public
docs.text:
Because the source repository is private and the hosting repository is public, the deployment process must:

  • Build and encrypt the site inside the private repository
  • Publish only the encrypted output to the public repository
  • Authenticate securely across repositories

No source files are ever copied to the public repository.

docs.title: Authentication model
docs.text:
Publishing to the public repository is done using an organization-owned GitHub App, not a Personal Access Token.

The GitHub App:

  • Is owned by the organization, not a person
  • Is installed only on the public hosting repository
  • Has minimal permissions (contents: write)
  • Issues short-lived tokens used during deployment

GitHub App used: - docs-pages-publisher - Managed at: https://github.com/organizations/polariis-plus/settings/apps/docs-pages-publisher

This ensures the deployment process:

  • Continues to work even if contributors leave the organization
  • Follows GitHub’s recommended security model
  • Avoids long-lived, person-bound credentials

docs.title: GitHub Pages hosting
docs.text:
The public repository is configured to serve GitHub Pages from a dedicated branch containing the encrypted site.

As a result:

  • GitHub Pages sees a normal public static site
  • Visitors are prompted for a password before accessing content
  • The documentation source remains private at all times

docs.title: Security considerations
docs.text:
This setup provides content obfuscation and access friction, not strong access control.

  • Anyone with the password can access the content
  • Encrypted files are publicly downloadable
  • This is appropriate for:
  • internal documentation
  • partner documentation
  • non-sensitive technical material

It is not intended for secrets or regulated data.

docs.title: Writing documentation with MkDocs & Material
docs.text:
This documentation is built with MkDocs and the Material for MkDocs theme.

The goal is to make documentation: - easy to write - easy to review - easy to keep up to date

This page introduces the basics and provides concrete examples you can reuse when adding or updating documentation.

docs.title: What is MkDocs?
docs.text:
MkDocs is a static documentation generator:

  • Documentation is written in Markdown
  • Pages are converted into a static website
  • Navigation is defined explicitly
  • No framework or frontend knowledge required

If you can write Markdown, you can write documentation.

docs.title: What is Material for MkDocs?
docs.text:
Material for MkDocs is a theme that adds:

  • Clean, modern UI
  • Built-in search
  • Responsive layout
  • Syntax highlighting
  • Callouts, tabs, diagrams, and more

It allows us to keep documentation simple, while still being pleasant and powerful.

docs.title: Where documentation lives
docs.text:
Documentation files live in the repository under:

projects/docs/pages/

Each Markdown file corresponds to one page in the site.

Example:

projects/docs/pages/
├────────────────── index.md
├────────────────── publishing-docs.md
└────────────────── writing-docs.md

Navigation and ordering are controlled in projects/docs/mkdocs.yml.

docs.title: POLARIIS+: Overview
docs.text:
POLARIIS+ is a collaborative, open, and evolutive life cycle database of lifestyles in Canada. Its mission is to provide high‑quality, transparent, and regionalized life cycle inventory (LCI) and impact assessment (LCIA) data to support decision‑making toward more sustainable lifestyles at the individual, organizational, and governmental levels.

POLARIIS+ is developed jointly by researchers and partners across Canada, with the goal of democratizing access to environmental footprint information while ensuring methodological rigor, interoperability, and future‑proof design.

docs.title: Why POLARIIS+?
docs.text:
Traditional LCA databases often focus on production-based inventories. However, to address the environmental footprint of households, public services, and societal trends, a consumption‑based approach is essential. This perspective evaluates the impacts of what is consumed in a territory, including imported goods and services.

Canada currently lacks:

  • Regionalized and lifestyle‑oriented LCA data
  • Fine‑granularity datasets reflecting everyday consumption
  • Parametric, flexible datasets enabling scenario and sensitivity analysis
  • Open, transparent datasets
  • Tools that are interoperable, machine‑readable to easy to update as new knowledge emerges and structure suitable for automation, AI, and digital tools and
  • A collaborative ecosystem for contributions, updates, and versioning

POLARIIS+ is designed to fill these gaps.

docs.title: Project Objectives
docs.text:
POLARIIS+ aims to structure and disseminate LCI and footprint data to:

  • Support evidence‑based decisions for citizens, companies, NGOs, and governments
  • Enable modeling of behaviour‑based scenarios
  • Provide a robust basis for public policies, organizational sustainability strategies, and educational initiatives
  • Empower citizens and professionals with open, accurate, and reproducible knowledge
  • Foster large‑scale collaborations and co‑creation of data across Canada

The platform will ultimately offer a versatile, modular, parametrized, and open framework capable of evolving with time, data contributions, and new scientific advances.

docs.title: Holistic Coverage
docs.text:
• Full life cycles including production and consumption
  • Multisectoral: food, transport, housing, digital services, health and personal care, culture, clothing, and more

docs.title: Regionalization
docs.text:
• Canada-wide
  • Provincial granularity (Québec, other provinces)
  • Distinction between domestic production and imports

docs.title: Versatility
docs.text:
• Multiple functional units and user profiles
  • Different levels of detail (items → recipes → meals → diets)
  • Multivariate contribution analysis

docs.title: Flexibility
docs.text:
• Parameterized datasets
  • Modular structure enabling the addition, removal, or adjustment of processes
  • Ontology-based modelling
  • Generic, reusable templates
  • Consistent parameter inheritance

docs.title: Collaboration & Interoperability
docs.text:
• Designed for data contributors, users, and partners
  • Compatible with external LCI databases and LCA software
  • API-based integration and machine-readable formats
  • Open access to foster participation and transparency

docs.title: Evolutiveness
docs.text:
• Version control
  • Branching capabilities for alternative modelling options
  • Capacity to incorporate new datasets over time

docs.title: Scope and System Boundaries
docs.text:
POLARIIS+ connects detailed consumption modelling (behaviours, choices, profiles) with production processes using a structured, harmonized process tree. Examples include:

  • For food: items → recipes → meals → diets, with detailed agricultural production, processing, packaging, transport, distribution, and end‑of‑life.
  • For transport: mobility behaviours, vehicle technologies, energy sources, and infrastructure.
  • For housing: buildings, energy use, materials.

The database interfaces with background LCI databases to complete full life cycle modelling.

docs.title: Multi-Dimensional Coverage
docs.text:
• Consumption sectors: transport, housing, food, travel, culture, clothing, health, finance, education, communication, public services, etc.
  • Environmental indicators: based on IMPACT World+ covering carbon footprint, water footprint, mineral and fossil resource use, human health, ecosystem quality
  • User needs and profiles: lifestyles, activity patterns, and behavioural assumptions relevant to Canadians

POLARIIS+ aims to represent the annual needs of Canadians through a comprehensive consumption-based lens.

docs.title: Methodology and Tools
docs.text:
Dataset creation follows a structured methodology:

  1. Definition of functional units relevant to lifestyles
  2. Ontologies for objects, processes, and impacts
  3. Harmonized process trees across sectors
  4. Prioritization of high-impact or high‑volume items
  5. Parameter development and equations
  6. Structured data collection templates
  7. Activity instantiation with validation and rules
  8. Dissemination through a web platform, APIs, documentation, and scientific outputs

This approach ensures consistency, transparency, and reproducibility.

docs.title: Current Progress
docs.text:
The following sectors are under active development:

  • Food: existing beta version
  • Transport
  • Housing existing beta version
  • Digital services
  • Hygiene and personal care existing beta version

Work is ongoing to expand sectoral coverage, incorporate new contributors, and refine licensing models.

docs.title: Collaboration and Governance
docs.text:
POLARIIS+ is built as a collaborative ecosystem involving:

  • Data contributors (experts, institutions, researchers, public agencies)
  • Direct and indirect users (LCA practitioners, analysts, policymakers, educators)
  • Financial contributors
  • A development team responsible for the LCI database and the footprint database structures, tools, and integration

Strong partnerships help ensure data quality, representativeness, and long-term viability.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
Upcoming priorities include:

  • Increasing the number and scope of datasets
  • Expanding collaborations and partnerships
  • Clarifying licensing with background databases
  • Improving tools for users and contributors
  • Strengthening the API ecosystem and documentation

docs.title: Méthode POLARIIS+
docs.text:
Statut : 🟡 Au chaud

Le squelette de cette documentation est en cours de construction (ticket Trello « Créer squelette documentation POLARIIS », liste En cours). L'organisation décrite ici est stabilisée ; le contenu de chaque section s'enrichit session après session.

docs.title: En bref
docs.text:
Cette section rassemble tout ce que l'équipe sait, a décidé, ou laisse encore ouvert sur la méthode POLARIIS+ : le vocabulaire, le modèle de données, les gestes du modélisateur, les algorithmes, les livrables. Elle est écrite pour deux lecteurs : le modélisateur ACV qui doit produire des datasets dans le template, et le nouvel arrivant qui doit comprendre pourquoi le modèle est construit ainsi.

Deux principes de lecture gouvernent l'ensemble :

  • Un workflow dit dans quel ordre, une notion dit comment. Les pages de workflows sont des suites d'étapes qui renvoient aux notions ; les pages de notion expliquent le mécanisme sans redire l'ordre.
  • Chaque page porte un statut. Rien n'est présenté comme acquis s'il ne l'est pas. Une page honnêtement vide vaut mieux qu'une page plausible et fausse.

docs.title: Comment cette section est organisée
docs.text: Sous-section Ce qu'elle couvre workflows/ Les parcours : les séquences qui traversent plusieurs notions. Monter une base sectorielle, créer un dataset de A à Z, construire une ontologie, le quotidien du modélisateur, reprendre le modèle de quelqu'un d'autre, publier une version. modele/ Le modèle conceptuel : vocabulaire et nommage, ontologie (dimensions, modalités, taxonomies), profils, activités et flux, compositions et ensembles, arbre de procédé, liaisons, paramètres, système de produit. C'est la sous-section la plus fournie — c'est là que vivent les définitions. donnees/ La matière : schéma et identifiants, versionnement, template Excel (guide, carte des feuilles, formulaires, import batch, gel structurel), contribution, qualité et métadonnées, validation. algorithmes/ Ce que fait la machine : instanciation, résolution des paramètres, qualité et incertitude, calcul et export Brightway, analyses d'agrégation/désagrégation, formats d'export. livrables/ Ce que la plateforme rend : personas et niveaux d'accès, librairie de modèles, visualisations, exports, analyses de contribution. exemples/ Les cas déroulés de bout en bout : jus d'orange, véhicule, repas. Ce sont les fils rouges de l'équipe. registre/ La mémoire du projet : décisions actées, questions ouvertes, idées à ne pas perdre, options écartées avec leur raison, chronologie. glossaire.md Le vocabulaire de référence, en un seul endroit.

docs.title: Comment lire une page
docs.text: Toutes les pages ont le même sommaire : En bref (autoportant), Ce que c'est (la définition), Comment ça marche (le mécanisme), Comment on le fait (le geste), Questions ouvertes, Écarté, Historique. Quand une section est vide, elle reste affichée avec la mention Rien de consigné pour l'instant — le sommaire de droite ne bouge jamais d'une page à l'autre.

docs.title: La légende des six statuts
docs.text:
Chaque page s'ouvre par un bandeau de statut. Ces statuts sont repris des documents de conception, qui marquent déjà leurs sections ; ils ne sont pas réévalués au moment de la rédaction.

Emoji Libellé Ce que ça veut dire 🟢 Acté Décidé et validé dans les sources. Entre dans le gel structurel. Ne pas rouvrir sans raison forte. 🟡 Au chaud Conceptuellement validé, mais pas encore figé dans une structure. Pas bloquant. 🔴 Ouvert Vrai travail de design restant. Ne bloque pas le gel (le sujet vit dans des cellules d'expression ou des feuilles additives), mais doit être traité avant l'implémentation complète. ⚠️ Angle mort Risque identifié, non encore résolu. À surveiller. 💡 Idée Pas travaillé, consigné pour ne pas le perdre. 🗄️ Écarté Envisagé puis abandonné — toujours accompagné de sa raison.

Les mêmes emojis servent à l'intérieur des pages : dans la section Questions ouvertes, chaque ligne est préfixée de 🔴, ⚠️ ou 💡 ; dans Écarté, de 🗄️.

docs.title: Où mettre une nouvelle idée
docs.text:
La règle de routage, selon la nature de ce qu'on a en main :

Ce que j'ai Où ça va Une définition — ce qu'est une chose, comment elle se comporte dans modele/, sur la page de la notion Une séquence d'étapes qui reste dans une seule notion dans la page de cette notion, section Comment on le fait Une séquence d'étapes qui traverse plusieurs notions dans workflows/ Une structure de données : feuille, colonne, identifiant, règle de saisie ou de validation dans donnees/ Un traitement fait par la machine : résolution, calcul, agrégation, conversion dans algorithmes/ Une sortie destinée à un utilisateur : visualisation, export, niveau d'accès dans livrables/ Un cas concret déroulé dans exemples/ Une décision datée, une question ouverte, une idée, une option abandonnée dans registre/ — et en écho dans la section correspondante de la page de la notion concernée

Le registre ne remplace pas les pages de notion, il les indexe. Une question ouverte vit dans la section Questions ouvertes de la page qui la concerne, et se retrouve listée dans registre/questions-ouvertes.md. Une option abandonnée vit dans la section Écarté de sa page, avec sa raison, et se retrouve dans registre/ecartees.md. Une raison perdue est une décision qu'on rouvrira pour rien.
